extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students studying linear algebra and linear systems (differential equations)
extracted.subtask_short: matrix canonical forms and linear systems
extracted.subtask_description: Canonical forms and classification of real n×n matrices (distinct, repeated, and complex eigenvalues), and using eigen-decomposition to solve linear ODE systems X' = AX. Includes definitions of subspace, basis, dimension, and rank-nullity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristic equation and eigenvalues
rubrics_metrics.description: The eigenvalues of A are the roots of det(A - λI). Example: expand det(A-λI) along a row/column to factor and obtain eigenvalues (e.g. det(A - λI) = (1-λ)(λ-2)(λ+1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute det(A-λI), factor the polynomial, and read off eigenvalues; expansion along any row or column is valid (see Exercises). The textbook demonstrates explicit expansion and factoring in examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eigenvector computation from (A - λI)X = 0
rubrics_metrics.description: For each eigenvalue λ solve the linear system (A - λI)X = 0 to obtain eigenvectors associated to λ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Row-reduce (A-λI) to find free variables and a basis for the nullspace; examples show reduction to simple relations (e.g. x = 3z, y = 2z, etc.) and exhibit explicit eigenvectors like (3,2,1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex eigenvalues occur in conjugate pairs for real matrices
rubrics_metrics.description: If α + iβ (β ≠ 0) is an eigenvalue of a real matrix A, then its complex conjugate α − iβ is also an eigenvalue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via taking complex conjugates of the eigen-equation AV = (α + iβ)V: conjugating gives AV̄ = (α − iβ)V̄. Consequence: complex eigenvalues come in pairs and produce real 2×2 blocks in canonical form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real and imaginary parts of complex eigenvectors form real vectors
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a complex eigenvector V for α + iβ, the real part Re V and imaginary part Im V are real vectors (W_{2j-1}, W_{2j}) that can be used as basis vectors in R^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define W_{2j-1}=(V+V̄)/2 and W_{2j} = -i(V - V̄)/2; these are real and, when collected over distinct complex eigenpairs, are linearly independent (proof by forming complex linear combinations and using independence of V and V̄). They bring us back to R^n and lead to 2×2 canonical blocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical 2×2 block for a complex eigenpair
rubrics_metrics.description: Each distinct nonreal eigenvalue α_j ± iβ_j produces a 2×2 real block D_j = [[α_j, β_j],[-β_j, α_j]] in the real canonical form of A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After choosing real basis vectors as real/imaginary parts of complex eigenvectors and performing the change of coordinates T, the matrix T^{-1}AT has diagonal 2×2 blocks D_j of the form [α β; -β α], representing rotation-dilation in the corresponding plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Block-diagonalization/diagonalization for distinct eigenvalues
rubrics_metrics.description: If an n×n matrix A has distinct eigenvalues, one can choose T so that T^{-1}AT is block-diagonal with 1×1 blocks for real eigenvalues and 2×2 blocks D_j for nonreal conjugate pairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theorem states T^{-1}AT = diag(λ_1, ..., λ_{k}, D_1, ..., D_m) where each D_j is a 2×2 block. For purely real distinct eigenvalues this reduces to a diagonal matrix. Columns of T are eigenvectors or real/imaginary parts of eigenvectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: subspace, span, and basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Given vectors V_1,...,V_k in R^n, the span S = {α_1V_1+...+α_kV_k} is a subspace. A collection V_1,...,V_k is a basis of S if they are linearly independent and span S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the spanning set is linearly dependent, remove extraneous vectors to obtain a basis. Every subspace has a basis by selecting independent vectors from a spanning set.

rubrics_metrics.name: All bases of a subspace have the same cardinality (dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every basis of a given subspace S ⊂ R^n has the same number of elements; this number is defined as dim S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by considering two bases of different sizes and expressing one basis in terms of the other to reach a contradiction (linear dependence). Consequence: dimension is well-defined; dim R^n = n and dim{0}=0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kernel and Range are subspaces; columns span the Range
rubrics_metrics.description: For a linear map T: R^n → R^n, Ker T = {v | Tv = 0} and Range T = {Tv | v∈R^n} are subspaces. The columns of the matrix of T lie in Range T and span it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: compute Ker via solving AX=0, Range via the column space; if columns are independent then Ker T = {0} and T is onto R^n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rank-nullity theorem (dimension relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: For linear T: R^n → R^n, dim Ker T + dim Range T = n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof given by extending a basis of Ker T to a basis of R^n and showing images of the remaining basis vectors are linearly independent and span Range T. Corollary: T is invertible iff dim Ker T = 0 (equivalently dim Range T = n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical forms for matrices with repeated eigenvalues (block description)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any n×n matrix A can be put (by change of coordinates) into a block-diagonal canonical form with blocks B_j that are either Jordan-like blocks for real eigenvalues or 2×2 blocks C_2 for complex eigenpairs; special cases include 1×1 blocks (λ) or a single C_2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposition lists allowed block shapes, including Jordan chains with 1s on a superdiagonal and repeated 2×2 C_2 blocks for complex eigenvalues. The general classification reduces problems to these block types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of 3×3 matrices with a single eigenvalue λ
rubrics_metrics.description: If a 3×3 matrix has λ as its only eigenvalue, then after change of coordinates T^{-1}AT must be one of three forms: (i) λI (three independent eigenvectors), (ii) a block with one Jordan 2×2 block and one 1×1 block (kernel dim 2), or (iii) a single Jordan chain (kernel dim 1) giving a full 3×3 Jordan block with superdiagonal ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide by examining dim Ker(A−λI): 3→(i), 2→(ii), 1→(iii). The text gives constructive proofs and examples showing how to pick generalized eigenvectors V2, V3 satisfying (A−λI)V2 = V1, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing generalized eigenvectors (Jordan chains)
rubrics_metrics.description: When there are insufficient independent eigenvectors, find generalized eigenvectors by solving (A−λI)X = V_k where V_k is an existing eigenvector or previously found generalized eigenvector to build a chain (A−λI)^m V = 0 with appropriate lengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: for case (iii) in 3×3, pick V1 in Ker(A−λI), then find V2 with (A−λI)V2 = V1, and V3 with (A−λI)V3 = V2, so that (A−λI)^2V3 = V1; use these to build a basis giving the Jordan form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical forms for 4×4 matrices with repeated complex eigenvalues
rubrics_metrics.description: For 4×4 matrices with repeated complex eigenvalues α ± iβ (β ≠ 0), either there are two independent eigenvectors leading to two 2×2 blocks, or only one eigenvector and then a block has superdiagonal 1s (generalized eigenvector) producing a 4×4 canonical arrangement mixing C_2 blocks and 1s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: find complex eigenvectors and conjugates, convert to real W basis (Re/Im parts), and if needed solve (A−(α+iβ)I)X = V to find generalized eigenvectors; placing TE_j = W_j yields the real canonical block form (with possible ones indicating Jordan chains across 2×2 blocks). Examples in the text illustrate both cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genericity: matrices with distinct eigenvalues are open and dense
rubrics_metrics.description: The set M of matrices in L(R^n) that have n distinct eigenvalues is open and dense in L(R^n); having n distinct eigenvalues is therefore a generic property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Density: perturb Jordan blocks or 2×2 C_2 blocks slightly to split repeated eigenvalues into distinct ones; openness: small changes in entries cause small changes in polynomial coefficients and thus small changes in roots, so distinctness persists nearby. Conclusion: 'most' matrices have distinct eigenvalues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solving linear systems X' = AX via eigen-decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: If A has n distinct real eigenvalues, change coordinates Y = T^{-1}X to decouple the system to y'_j = λ_j y_j; solutions are y_j(t) = c_j e^{λ_j t} and X(t)=Σ c_j e^{λ_j t} V_j.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When complex eigenpairs occur, use real/imaginary parts to obtain real solutions of the form e^{αt}(p cos βt + q sin βt). The columns of T are eigenvectors or real/imaginary parts of eigenvectors and determine the general solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stable and unstable subspaces; hyperbolic systems
rubrics_metrics.description: If eigenvalues split by sign of real parts (λ_1,...,λ_k negative, λ_{k+1},...,λ_n positive) with no zero eigenvalues, the system is hyperbolic. The subspace spanned by eigenvectors with negative real parts is the stable subspace (solutions tend to origin), and the one spanned by positive real parts is the unstable subspace (solutions move away).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solutions starting in the stable subspace tend to the origin as t→∞; those in the unstable subspace go away from the origin; other solutions approach unstable subspace forward in time and stable backward. Examples show a saddle decomposition in R^3 with explicit eigenvectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real solutions from complex eigenpairs (spiral/center behaviour)
rubrics_metrics.description: A complex eigenpair α ± iβ produces two real solution components u(t), v(t) satisfying u' = α u + β v, v' = -β u + α v, and solutions u(t)=e^{αt}(a cos βt + b sin βt), v(t)=e^{αt}(-a sin βt + b cos βt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: α<0 gives spirals into origin, α=0 gives centers (pure rotations), α>0 gives spirals away. Use these paired real coordinates (from Re/Im parts) to understand phase portraits; examples include spiral centers and decay by e^{αt}.
